name: Qatabanic, a dialect of Ancient South Arabian
confidence_why: Nebes & Stein 2004, the standard reference description of Ancient South Arabian, state outright that no conclusions are possible about its accent, Kogan & Korotayev 1997 note that the purely consonantal script gives no direct information about vowels, and the Qatabanic lexica and corpus review read (Ricks 1982, 1989; Müller 2005) say nothing about stress, so the record that Qatabanic word stress…
catalog_citation: Nebes, Norbert & Peter Stein. 2004. 'Ancient South Arabian'. In Roger D. Woodard (ed.), The Cambridge Encyclopedia of the World's Ancient Languages, ch. 15, 454-487. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.
catalog_locator: sec. 3.3 'Vowels', pp. 458-459 (PDF pp. 482-483 of; saved chapter text the copy we)
catalog_quote: The few statements that can be made about the vocalization of Ancient South Arabian are based on the use of the glides w and y. The final writings of plural forms of verbs (Sab. hqnyw “they dedicated”), personal pronouns (hmw; -hw), and enclitic particles (-mw; -my) are in all likelihood to be read as vocalic (presumably as long /u:/ and /i:/). ... Apart from these few hints, practically nothing is known about the vocalization of the Ancient South Arabian texts preserved for us. The question of a possible differentiation of syllables according to vowel quantity, therefore, likewise cannot be answered with certainty, nor are any broad conclusions possible concerning the accentual relationships of Ancient South Arabian.
world_status: statement found in a copy we already had

new_statements.rule_in_words: No stress location can be stated: Qatabanic (like all Ancient South Arabian) is attested only in unvocalized consonantal script with no reading tradition, and the primary description says explicitly that no conclusions about accent are possible. This is a first-hand 'accent unknowable' statement, not a stress rule.
new_statements.exceptions: None. The only stress-related remark anywhere in the ASA literature opened is Kogan & Korotayev 1997: 224, a speculation that Minaic 'parasitic h' reflects 'a peculiar character of the stress (possibly even pitch)' -- Minaic, not Qatabanic.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about the whole Ancient South Arabian epigraphic corpus (four dialects incl. Qatabanic), not about word vs phrase domain; no citation forms exist (dead epigraphic language).
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding statement (Nebes & Stein 2004) is made for Ancient South Arabian as a whole (Sabaic, Minaic, Qatabanic, Hadramitic; chapter p. 454 names Qatabanic explicitly as one of the four dialects covered); it is not Qatabanic-specific. The same passage was used by sibling checks for hadr1235 (Hadramitic) and saba1279 (Sabaic). Qatabanic is an extinct epigraphic language (c. 7th c. BC - 2nd c. AD) written only in the unvocalized consonantal musnad script with no reading tradition, so no first-hand location of word stress can exist.
